title: Sabu M Varghese vs Vimala Rosy A.A on 21 October, 2022

paragraphs.text:
IN THE HIGH COURT OF KERALA AT ERNAKULAM
 PRESENT
 THE HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE ANIL K.NARENDRAN
 &
 THE HONOURABLE MR.JUSTICE P.G. AJITHKUMAR
FRIDAY, THE 21ST DAY OF OCTOBER 2022 / 29TH ASWINA, 1944
 MAT.APPEAL NO. 701 OF 2021
 AGAINST THE JUDGMENT DATED 31.08.2022 IN O.P.NO.200 OF
 2018 OF THE FAMILY COURT, ERNAKULAM
APPELLANT/PETITIONER:

 SABU M VARGHESE
 AGED 48 YEARS, S/O. VARGHESE, MANGALAPPILLY
 HOUSE, NO.43/406, EROOR WEST P.O,
 THRIPUNITHURA, ERNAKULAM DISTRICT.
 BY ADV JOSEPH M.P.


RESPONDENT/RESPONDENT:

 VIMALA ROSY A.A
 AGED 40 YEARS, W/O. SABU M VARGHESE,
 D/O. ANTONY, ADICHIYIL HOUSE, THYKOODAM,
 VYTILLA P.O, ERNAKULAM DISTRICT.


 BY ADV M.V.KISHORE KUMAR



 THIS MATRIMONIAL APPEAL HAVING COME UP FOR FINAL
HEARING ON 21.10.2022, THE COURT ON THE SAME DAY
DELIVERED THE FOLLOWING:
 2
Mat.Appeal No.701 of 2021


 JUDGMENT
Ajithkumar, J.

The petitioner in O.P.No.200 of 2018 on the file of the

Family Court, Ernakulam is the appellant. He filed the original

petition for dissolution of his marriage with the respondent on

the ground of desertion under Section 10(1)(ix) of the Divorce

Act, 1869. That petition was dismissed as per the judgment

dated 31.08.2021, which is under challenge in this appeal

filed under Section 19 of the Family Courts Act, 1984.
2. On 15.12.2021 this appeal was admitted.

3. Heard the learned counsel appearing for the

appellant and the learned counsel appearing for the

respondent.

4. Marriage of the appellant and the respondent was

solemnized on 15.04.2002. They have two daughters. The

appellant seeks dissolution of marriage on the basis of the

allegations that the respondent voluntarily left the

matrimonial home on 29.12.2013 and ever thereafter she has

not turned up to have cohabitation with the appellant.
 3
Mat.Appeal No.701 of 2021

5. The respondent resisted the petition contending

that she had to leave the company of the appellant since she

has been experiencing total neglect, mental and physical

cruelty and lack of support from the appellant. He never

discharged his marital obligations. It is contented that they

had to leave the family house where she along with the

appellant and the children were residing, following partition.

They shifted to a rented house, but had to often change the

rented house since the appellant was not prompt in making

payment of the rent. The money obtained during partition was

wasted by him. Although several businesses were attempted,

all ended up in loss due to his irresponsibility. He did not

bother to provide even food and shelter to the respondent as

well as the children. The gold ornaments and money given to

the respondent at the time of marriage were misappropriated.

He used to manhandle the respondent. She therefore filed a

complaint before the police, and M.C.No.16 of 2014 claiming

maintenance and other reliefs. Owing to the unbearable

miseries due to mental and physical cruelty she could not
 4
Mat.Appeal No.701 of 2021


continue cohabitation. Also, she along with children could not

continue in the rented house for want of payment of rent by

the respondent. It was in such circumstances she along with

the children left for her parental house. The respondent

accordingly sought to dismiss the petition.

6. PWs.1 to 4 were examined and Exts.A1 to A12

were marked on the side of the appellant. RWs.1 to 3 were

examined and Exts.B1 to B4 were marked on the side of the

respondent. The Family Court after considering the evidence

on record found that the respondent had to leave the

matrimonial home only on account of the fault on the part of

the appellant and in fact, it was the appellant who meted out

cruelty and if at all to claim divorce, it should have been by

the respondent. She still wanted to continue the marital

chord. The Family Court accordingly dismissed the petition.

7. The learned counsel appearing for the appellant

would submit that the Family Court was not correct in holding

that the evidence let in by the appellant was insufficient to

grant a decree of divorce. It is pointed out that the
 5
Mat.Appeal No.701 of 2021


respondent's leaving the matrimonial home on 29.12.2013 is

an admitted fact and the reasons stated by her for

abandoning the company of the appellant is unacceptable.

When Section 10(1)(ix) of the Divorce Act states that a

decree of divorce is liable to be granted if a spouse deserted

for a period of more than two years immediately preceding

the filing of the petition, it is incumbent upon the court to

grant such a decree since sufficient evidence in proof of such

desertion was placed before the court.

8. The respondent does not dispute that she left the

matrimonial home. The assertion of PW1 that she abandoned

the matrimonial home on 29.12.2013 is not challenged. The

learned counsel for the respondent contended that mere

leaving from the marital home does not amount to desertion.

He asserts that if a spouse leaves the marital tie for justifiable

reason that will not amount to desertion for the purpose of

 Section 10(1)(ix) of the Divorce Act. If a person is unable to

cope with the situation and forced to leave the home as a

result of the acts and deeds of the other spouse, that cannot
 6
Mat.Appeal No.701 of 2021


be an abandonment, but it involves a forceful ousting from

the home. The learned counsel would submit that the

evidence sufficiently established that the respondent left the

house only because of the miseries she and her children had

to face on account of the misdeeds of the appellant and hence

the judgment of the Family Court does not suffer from any

vice.

9. As against the oral testimony of PW1 that the

respondent failed to discharge her responsibilities as a wife

and left the home without any justifiable reason, the

respondent deposed as RW1 narrating the circumstances in

which she had to leave the home. It is her version that only

on account of aid and help from the uncle of the appellant,

she could live on for a considerable period in the company of

the appellant and the appellant never had looked after the

affairs of herself or the children.

10. Ext.A9 series, A11 and A12 were produced to show

that certain amounts were paid to the respondent and thus

the appellant has met the expenses relating to the
 7
Mat.Appeal No.701 of 2021


maintenance of the wife and children. The payments

evidenced by the said documents were by the mother and

uncle of the appellant. The evidence of RWs.2 and 3 assumes

much importance in that context.

11. RW2 is the sister and RW3 is the brother-in-law of

the appellant. Going by their versions, it is quite evident that

the appellant never was responsible in the affairs of not only

the wife, but also children. He was a spent-thrift and drunkard

showing no interest or regard to the affairs of the children.

When his own sister and brother-in-law describe the appellant

as such a man, how could the respondent along with her two

daughters, who are aged 13 and 8 years, continue to live with

the appellant. RW1 deposed that the appellant did not even

pay rent for their rented accommodation, he did not meet the

expenses of the daily sustenance and education of the

children and he used to torture her even physically. Those

versions were not successfully cross-examined.

12. PW2 is the Doctor who was consulted by the

appellant and the respondent together. Ext.A4 is a medical
 8
Mat.Appeal No.701 of 2021


prescription. From the evidence of PW2, it is seen that the

appellant was an addict of alcohol, tobacco and drugs. In the

view of PW2 the behavioural pattern and abnormality on the

part of the appellant resulted in mental stress and depression

to the respondent, and other than that, she has no issues for

leading a healthy married life. Thus the evidence brought on

record established that the respondent was subjected to

intolerable cruelty, both physical and mental. On the other

hand, the appellant did not adduce any evidence to

probabilise that the respondent voluntarily had left the

matrimonial home and thereby deserted the appellant.

13. The term 'desertion' is defined in Section 3(9) of

the Divorce Act. 'Desertion' implies an abandonment against

the wish of the person charging it. Therefore, against the wish

of the person, who alleges such abandonment will amount to

desertion. But abandonment shall not be one that forced the

spouse to leave the home as a result of the acts and deeds of

the other spouse, that cannot be an abandonment, but it is a

forceful ousting from the home. An abandonment is a
 9
Mat.Appeal No.701 of 2021


voluntary act. If leaving the house is the only option available

to the spouse, the same cannot be an abandonment.

14. In Lachman Utamchand Kirpalani v. Meena @

Mota [1964 (4) SCR 331] the Apex Court explained the term

desertion and that principle has been consistently followed in

several decisions of the Apex Court. The law consistently laid

down is that desertion means the intentional abandonment of

one spouse by the other without the consent of the other and

without a reasonable cause. The deserted spouse must prove

that there is a factum of separation and there is an intention on

the part of the deserting spouse to bring the cohabitation to a

permanent end. In other words, there should be animus

deserendi on the part of the deserting spouse. There must be an

absence of consent on the part of the deserted spouse and the

conduct of the deserted spouse should not give a reasonable

cause to the deserting spouse to leave the matrimonial home.

15. After referring to the said principle the Apex Court

in Debananda Tamuli v. Kakumoni Kataky [(2022) 5

SCC 459] held that the reasons for a dispute between
 10
Mat.Appeal No.701 of 2021


husband and wife are always very complex and every

matrimonial dispute is different from another. Whether a case

of desertion is established or not will depend on the peculiar

facts of each case. It is a matter of drawing an inference

based on the facts brought on record by way of evidence.

16. In Darshan Gupta v. Radhika Gupta [(2013) 9

SCC 1] it was held that merely because the husband and wife

are staying separately, an inference regarding desertion on

the wife's part cannot be drawn. It must be shown that

separation is wilful and deliberate. Desertion should be with

animus deserendi, meaning thereby, there must be a vicious

intention to part with the matrimonial company of the other

spouse and to deprive him or her of the matrimonial bliss. The

burden of proof is heavy on the person who seeks the relief of

divorce on the ground of desertion. The factum of separation,

intention to separate, absence of consent by the other spouse

and absence of his or her conduct driving the other to leave

the matrimonial home are to be established if one is to get a

decree of divorce.
Mat.Appeal No.701 of 2021

17. We are of the view that the evidence let in by the

appellant is totally insufficient to establish that the respondent

deserted the marital company of the appellant voluntarily. If

the evidence adverted to above is viewed in the light of the

aforementioned principle of law, we are of the view that the

desertion of the appellant is for just and sufficient cause and

the appellant failed to prove the requirements of Section

10(1)(ix) of the Divorce Act. The Family Court considered all

the relevant evidence that came on record and rightly

concluded that the evidence was totally insufficient to grant a

decree of dissolution of marriage on the ground of desertion.

We find no reason to interfere with the said finding.
Therefore, this appeal fails and the same is dismissed.
Sd/-

ANIL K. NARENDRAN, JUDGE


 Sd/-

P.G. AJITHKUMAR, JUDGE
